entities.name: Church of San Cernín, Pamplona
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of San Cernín (also Church of San Saturnino, named for Saint Saturninus of Toulouse), a 13th-14th century Gothic church in Pamplona, Navarre, Spain, is one of the most historically significant churches in the city — traditionally the site where the Pamplona population first received Christian baptism (from Saint Saturninus, Bishop of Toulouse, who visited circa 3rd century CE), one of the Pamplona churches serving pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago, and possessing notable Gothic architecture with a fortified character (twin towers) reflecting Pamplona's medieval status as a contested frontier city.

Saint Saturninus (San Saturnino, San Cernín in Navarrese) is the Apostle of Navarre — the missionary bishop credited with bringing Christianity to Pamplona and baptizing its first converts in the well within the church's precinct. The tradition of the first Pamplona baptism at San Cernín makes the church a founding religious monument of Navarrese Christianity. Saint Saturninus was later martyred in Toulouse (tied to a bull and dragged through the streets), and his cult connects Pamplona to the broader Pyrenean-Toulouse religious tradition.

Pamplona's famous Running of the Bulls (Encierro de San Fermín) — the centerpiece of the Festival of San Fermín — honors Pamplona's other patron saint, San Fermín (the first bishop of Pamplona, a disciple of Saturninus). The festival and the bull-running make Pamplona globally famous. The Church of San Cernín, as home of Navarre's Christian founding saint, stands at the beginning of this tradition — Saturninus taught Fermín, who was later martyred, whose festival became the internationally famous Running of the Bulls.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of San Cernín Pamplona — founding religious monument of Navarrese Christianity through Saturninus's baptism tradition, Gothic fortified landmark on the Camino de Santiago, and beginning of the apostolic chain leading to the globally famous Festival of San Fermín — is historically significant for its foundational role in Navarre's religious identity.
